tagline: Seal colonies, a working lighthouse and an old alignment mark the coast road.
intro: Highway 1 follows the San Francisco Peninsula’s west coast through San Mateo County, passing Año Nuevo and Pigeon Point on its way toward Half Moon Bay. At Pescadero, sandy coves, rocky cliffs and tide pools lie beside the highway, with the marsh preserve across the road. San Gregorio’s coastal climate brings frequent night and morning fog, especially in summer; conditions a few miles inland are often warmer.

California extended legislative Route 56 north along the coast from Carmel through Santa Cruz to San Francisco in 1933. The road’s alignment kept changing: Highway 1 once passed through Purissima, while the present highway lies farther west. At Pescadero Creek, the bridge was rebuilt in 1989–90 closer to the ocean, with fewer supports to reduce its effects on the stream and lagoon. That project replaced a bridge built in the early 1940s, another stage in the coast road’s development.

Heading north, begin with Año Nuevo’s marine mammal colonies and the white tower at Pigeon Point. Pescadero State Beach comes before San Gregorio, whose village stands one mile inland on Highway 84. Near Verde Road, the Purissima town site lies four miles south of Half Moon Bay, beside an earlier alignment of the highway.

moments.title: Año Nuevo
moments.text: Northern elephant seals breed on the beaches and dunes of Año Nuevo, a low, rocky point projecting into the Pacific. Hunters greatly reduced their numbers, but the population rebounded from the mid-twentieth century. The park now supports one of the largest mainland breeding colonies of the species. During breeding season, males battle for mates on the beaches while females give birth on the dunes. Most adults leave by mid-March, while weaned pups remain through April. Females return in spring and males in summer to molt. The park also encompasses freshwater marsh and streamside red alder forest, with wetlands that support California red-legged frogs.

moments.title: Pigeon Point Lighthouse
moments.text: Pigeon Point’s white masonry tower rises 115 feet above its base on a rocky promontory. Built in 1871 to guide coastal shipping, it took its name from the Carrier Pigeon, wrecked here in 1853. Its Fresnel lens was first lit here on November 15, 1872. The original lamp burned lard oil; kerosene followed, then electricity in 1926. Originally, clockwork and a 45-pound weight powered the lens’s rotation. The Coast Guard retired the lens from regular duty in 1972, and it was moved to the fog-signal building in 2011. A separate beacon keeps the station working as a navigation aid.

moments.title: Purissima
moments.text: Verde Road follows an old alignment of Highway 1 through the Purissima area. The town developed in an agricultural district in the early 1850s and had a post office, stores, a school and a hotel by the early 1870s. A mill processed redwood timber from the nearby Santa Cruz Mountains. The Ocean Shore Railroad later stopped here, but the town was largely abandoned before World War II. Highway 1 now runs farther west; the cemetery remains in woods between the highway and Verde Road. Work to clear the cemetery and its access trails began in 2017.
